subject: Creativity
title: Random Entry: Forcing Unexpected Connections
description: A 60-second lesson on Random Entry: Forcing Unexpected Connections.

hook.text: Open a dictionary to a random word. Now connect it to your problem. This isn't chaos — it's de Bono's Random Entry.

buildup.text: Your brain is a pattern-matching machine. Given any two concepts, it will find a connection — even if none exists.

discovery.text: The random word forces your thinking into unfamiliar territory — the same territory where original ideas live.

twist.text: The technique works because bad connections are impossible. Your brain will always find something — and it's often.

climax.text: A hospital used 'race car' as random input for patient flow. Result: pit-stop model for emergency room handoffs.

punchline.text: Randomness isn't the enemy of creativity. It's the shortcut.

quiz.question: Why does the Random Entry technique work?
options: The brain automatically finds connections between any two concepts

details.summary: Random entry introduces an arbitrary word or image into a creative challenge and forces connections between the random element and the problem. The technique works because the brain is wired to find patterns and meaning even in unrelated pairings.
details.whyItMatters: Random entry is one of the simplest and most reliable creative techniques. It produces surprising connections by exploiting the brain's compulsive pattern-finding, making it impossible to think the same old thoughts.
takeaways: A random word or image is introduced as a creative catalyst
The brain automatically seeks connections to the problem
The technique breaks habitual thinking patterns reliably

faq.question: How do you choose the random word?
faq.answer: The word should be truly random, not selected for relevance. Open a dictionary to a random page, use a random word generator, or point blindly at a newspaper. The less related the word is to the problem, the more novel the connections will be.

faq.question: Does random entry actually work?
faq.answer: Yes. Studies show it consistently produces more original ideas than unaided brainstorming. The technique works because any word activates a unique web of associations in the brain that would not otherwise connect to the problem.
